The Lake City Broncos fall basketball program drew players ages 10 to 17, with U14 and U17 girls team and U13, U15, and U17 boys team. The Lake City Broncos recognized players and thanked their youth coaches at the fall awards night on Nov. 12. Each team handed out three awards. The Lake City Broncos U17 girls reached the final and U14 girls picked up a win on their first trip to Vancouver area as an age group. The Lake City Broncos have wrapped up their biggest fall season yet, fielding five travel teams and sending each one to the Vancouver area to compete. The Williams Lake program drew players ages 10 to 17, with U14 and U17 girls’ teams and U13, U15, and U17 boys’ teams, said coach Travis Nystoruk. Nystoruk said all five teams competed even though fall is typically the Broncos’ shorter season, with fewer tournaments to choose from than in spring. The Broncos travelled to Kelowna, Kamloops and the Vancouver area during the season. Their early trips included a late-September tournament hosted by GW Hoops in Kelowna. In October, the U15 and U17 boys travelled to Langley and Surrey for the DRIVE Fall Classic. The U15 boys reached the silver division final, losing by two points, while the U17 boys finished in a three-way tie for second in their round-robin pool. Nystoruk said the U15 boys had been training with the program for several years and its run to the silver division final showed how far it had come against teams from the Vancouver area. At the Remembrance Day Jamboree, the U17 girls reached the final and the U14 girls picked up a win on their first trip to the Vancouver area as an age group. The Broncos girls’ team attended a skills camp with national team player Taya Hanson and former head coach of the University of Manitoba women’s basketball team, Pam Danis, in Chilliwack. Premier Lorne Doerkson speaks to media following the swearing in of his cabinet in Victoria on Nov. 20, 2026. Premier Lorne Doerkson plans to hit the ground running on several campaign pledges, including implementing a promised tax cut as soon as Jan. 1. Doerkson laid out his agenda and explained some of his cabinet choices at his first press conference as premier, shortly after Lt.-Gov. Wendy Cocchia swore him in on Friday, Nov. 20. He said Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity resources in schools, an anti-bullying program known as SOGI 123, will be done away with immediately. However, Doerkson has still not explained how this will work in practice. The new government also plans a comprehensive review of the province’s finances, which new Finance Minister Peter Milobar says will begin in the coming weeks. Other thorny issues like his plans to repeal the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act will need to wait until the legislature convenes in the spring. “I’m absolutely committed to repealing DRIPA because it hasn’t solved our problems,” he said. The promised tax cut was a signature campaign promise for Doerkson. But without a fall legislative session, the new government can’t pass the necessary bill before the new year. Doerkson said he hopes to implement the tax changes in the spring legislative session, and backdate it to Jan. 1. The proposal, which the Conservative Party laid out in its campaign platform, is to increase the personal provincial income tax exemption from $13,216 to more than $32,000, providing an effective tax credit of $1,000 for everyone earning that amount or more. This only fully benefits those who earn at least $32,000 per year. People earning less get a smaller benefit, and those without income get nothing. e4126ca92dc2df001fbf9f2c564e589c.text: The Okanagan Falls branch of the Royal Canadian Legion has temporarily shut down, according to a letter shared to the organization’s social media on Nov. 19. According to the letter, BC/Yukon Command of the Royal Canadian Legion has suspended Branch #227’s bylaws and powers, stood down its current executive, and appointed two trustees to act on its behalf. The letter is signed by BC/Yukon president Robert Underhill. The Penticton Western News contacted the BC/Yukon Command on Nov. 19, but has not yet received a reply with additional information. “Despite the support and direction provided during Trusteeship Level 1, ongoing concerns remain regarding the Branch’s financial and operational management, governance and compliance with Legion policies and procedures,” reads the letter. “As these matters have not been sufficiently addressed, additional oversight is necessary to help bring the branch back into compliance and strengthen its overall operations.” This is the second B.C. branch to be placed under trusteeship, following Maple Ridge in September. The Maple Ridge Legion, Branch #88, is the largest in Canada with almost 5,000 members. The letter that was issued to Maple Ridge contains almost the same text as the letter issued to Okanagan Falls, including encouraging the members to continue to remain engaged and support the Branch while it is under trusteeship. More than a decade ago, Penticton Legion Branch #40 was placed under trusteeship for over three years, from 2012 to 2015. Premier Lorne Doerkson is continuing to appoint his MLAs to key roles, with the latest being his caucus leadership team. Doerkson said in a Friday (Nov. 20) news release that the Conservative caucus brings together dedicated representatives from communities across the province “who are ready to roll up their sleeves and get to work.” “This leadership team will play an important role in supporting our MLAs, strengthening our caucus and ensuring we remain focused on the priorities of the British Columbians we were elected to serve.” Surrey-White Rock MLA Trevor Halford has been named the government house leader. West Kelowna-Peachland MLA Macklin McCall was appointed as government whip, while Vancouver-Langara Jaime Stein is the deputy government whip. Doerkson told media following the swearing in of his cabinet that longtime Richmond-Bridgeport MLA Teresa Wat would be nominated for speaker. Canada’s defence minister has asked for a review of the country’s cadet program funding after concerns about cuts and pauses. National Defence Minister David McGuinty said Friday (Nov. 20) that his ministry has heard the concerns raised by cadets, families and communities across Canada about changes to planned activities. He said he will ensure the cadet community is kept informed as the review progresses. “We know how much this program means to young Canadians and the important role it plays in developing leadership, confidence, and a commitment to service.” McGuinty’s statement comes after days of news stories surrounding the state of the cadet and junior Canadian ranger programs amid budget constraints. The Ottawa Citizen first reported a pause for the program, citing an internal document. Some media outlets then reported suspensions or cancellations of cadet meetings. The Department of National Defence issued a statement Wednesday saying that spending was being reassessed and “adjustments” would be required for some planned activities. The department clarified the next day that the core cadet program is not changing, specifically that “adjustments are being made to specific additional activities outside of the core weekly programming.” McGuinty’s statement says the full budget for the cadets this year is $265 million, which is an increase from last year and previous years. “That investment reflects our strong commitment to the program. There will be no changes to core weekly programming.” He also noted that the 2026 Spring Economic Update announced $250 million over five years, starting in 2026–27, to expand Canada’s skilled trades training capacity through the Canadian Armed Forces and that included a $27-million increase for cadets this year. District of Barriere Mayor Rob Kerslake is seeking to spark a conversation about how infrastructure is funded in municipalities, and is pushing for change in the municipal finance system. The mayor of Barriere is looking to spark a conversation about precarious grant programs and stir up change in the municipal funding system in light of daunting critical infrastructure costs facing his town in the coming years. Mayor Rob Kerslake of the District of Barriere remarked that the infrastructure funding gap is not a new topic. “It’s been around for a while,” he said. “What we’re finding in Barriere is, as we dive deeper into our asset management, it tells a story that’s not so great. We have multi-million dollar projects that we have to fund, and you know, for a small town with 1,000 ratepayers, (it’s) near impossible.” A primary pillar of Kerslake’s concern is the precarity of relying on grants to fund such projects. In an attempt to address the issue, he brought a resolution to the Southern Interior Local Government Association (SILGA) convention this year to advocate for new revenue streams for municipalities. The resolution was endorsed by the Union of B.C. Municipalities (UBCM) and is listed in its 2026 Resolutions Book. It points to “significant infrastructure deficits” among local governments across B.C., noting that many are unable to meet needs through property taxes alone. The endorsed resolution calls on UBCM to advocate for the province of B.C. and the federal government to establish a revenue-sharing model that allocates a portion of PST and GST revenues collected within municipal boundaries and electoral areas to go directly back to local governments. The purpose of the new revenue streams would be designed to gradually reduce reliance on grant programs. The resolution

Police and B.C. conservation officers have confirmed that a black bear was destroyed last Saturday in Revelstoke, B.C., after finding food in an open garage and injuring a boy. The Conservation Officer Service (COS) confirmed with Black Press Media that the bear entered a residential garage in the Arrow Heights neighbourhood on Nov. 14. “Unaware that a bear was inside, a male youth approached the garage and attempted to close the access door,” it said in a statement. “The bear made contact with the youth, resulting in injuries.” With its nearest office being in Salmon Arm, the COS couldn’t attend the scene promptly and asked Revelstoke RCMP to respond. Officers from the detachment arrived to the property and found the bear still in the garage guarding non-natural food sources. Staff Sgt. Chris Dodds told Black Press Media the bear had already injured the 16-year-old boy by the time police were called. “In consultation with the BC Conservation Officer Service, the RCMP dispatched the bear due to public safety concerns,” the COS said. “The victim received medical attention for non-life threatening injuries.” Dodds said the COS eventually attended the scene as well to remove the destroyed bear, and is responsible for following up on the incident. He noted that RCMP was “acting on behalf of the conservation service” and receives numerous human-bear conflict calls every year. “We’ve had lots of bear complaints, right?” Dodds said. “There are attractants in neighbourhoods that they are attracted to.” He added that it’s not unusual for bears to still be visiting town this late in the fall — “it’s no different than any other year.” Kait Nicol, executive director of the Revelstoke Bear Aware Society,

e80bad78e6f0e9befa8a102fb9f50241.text: CNC Dental Clinic offers affordable care while supporting student learning. The College of New Caledonia (CNC) is inviting adults and children to access affordable dental hygiene services through its student-run clinic in Prince George. According to a press release by CNC, the clinic is accepting patients now and will operate until the end of April 2027. Services include dental X-rays and cleaning for a one-time fee of $50 for adults and $25 for children under 18. Patients may require more than one appointment depending on their dental health needs, but the fee remains the same regardless of the number of visits. “Regular dental care is an important part of maintaining overall health, but we recognize that cost can be a barrier for many individuals and families,” Diane Horita, Dental Hygiene Faculty and DS program coordinator at CNC, said. “Our clinic provides an opportunity for people to access affordable care while helping our students develop the clinical skills and confidence they need to become successful dental hygiene professionals. We especially welcome patients who haven’t had a dental appointment in a long time, as these experiences provide important learning opportunities for our students.” CNC also reminds potential patients that appointments take longer than those at a traditional clinic, as services are provided by students under faculty supervision. Patients should expect each visit to last between an hour and a half and three hours, and some treatments may require multiple visits. Despite the additional time commitment being an important factor to consider, the college also noted the clinic offers patients an opportunity to receive dental hygiene care at a significantly reduced cost while contributing directly to the education of future health-care professionals. “At CNC, we are committed to providing learning experiences that prepare students for successful careers while making a meaningful difference in our communities,” Stephanie Takeda,

b8815ba3de8be9e28e5b3a87703e1e35.text: Vanessa Moberg is the Cariboo Chilcotin Conservation Society's financial coordinator. After some recent decluttering Vanessa Moberg still kept a bag of tar sands, a sentimental reminder of her uncle and a practical reminder of the fossil fuels required to produce all her other stuff. Eager to declutter, I recently went through my boxes of sentimental items. “I’m a minimalist,” I thought. “This should be easy.” Before long, I found myself holding a Ziploc bag filled with a dark substance, and I thought, “Oh yeah! The tar sands my uncle gave me. Well, I can’t just throw out these perfectly good tar sands, now, can I?” I spent most of that day sitting on the basement floor surrounded by my “thing piles”: keep, store, donate, recycle. It was a thoroughly exhausting day filled with micro-decisions. Somehow, we develop a strong emotional attachment to a thing, even as the thing holds absolutely no purpose in our lives. We may remember buying it, how proud we were of it, the effort it took to acquire it, or the hopes we had for it. When we hold the thing in our hands again, all those emotions come flooding back, and we hesitate to get rid of it, even though it has spent the last decade relegated to a box, at the back of a closet, in the room no one goes into. There are health implications of having too many things. Studies have linked clutter to sleep disturbances, digestive problems, poor food choices, and even relationship issues. On the other hand, having clean, minimalist spaces can make one feel light, relaxed, organized, and more productive. Beyond the mental health effects, it takes a financial toll, not just to acquire things, but to maintain, insure, and store them. And then there are the environmental effects. Aside from the obvious end-of-life waste generated, most things require surprising amounts of resources to produce, transport, operate, and throw away, including water, chemicals, raw materials, and energy – often fossil fuels. 660204abef1dce5d4db9461d4fa2969e.text: The festive season is getting closer, and Quesnel residents can look forward to an evening of Moonlight Madness this month. Scheduled for Friday, Nov. 20, from 9 a.m. to 11 p.m., Moonlight Madness will once again offer an opportunity for community members to get out, explore local businesses, find great deals and get a head start on their Christmas shopping. The annual shopping event encourages residents to support local merchants while enjoying the excitement and atmosphere of the holiday shopping season. “It’s exciting as ever,” Lisa Foottit, head of the marketing committee for Quesnel Downtown Association (QDA), said. Foottit explained that participating businesses will have a poster on their window as well as entry forms for the draws of baskets of goods, organized by QDA. “There’s over $6,000 worth of donated prizes split between three baskets and a bonus basket this year,” she added. “The participating merchants have all been gracious and given something to put in, so that’s pretty exciting.” For Foottit, Moonlight Madness is a great way to kick off the holiday season shopping and have residents spend their dollars locally. “It’s just a really big time to promote shopping local, which is, in light of everything going on in the world and recently in our community, more important than ever,” she said. “The more money you spend locally, the more it stays in town. We have such amazing merchants that continue to support all the fundraisers and events that go on – from minor hockey to fundraisers when somebody’s sick. So, it’s important that our dollars stay here, so those businesses can continue to operate and help.” For those participating in Moonlight Madness for the first time or that are getting ready to participate in it again this year, Foottit hopes they all have a great time. “I just think it’s the greatest day of the year, honestly. af19f098f3c398d6344ec5be40d001cf.text: 100 Mile Ford is collecting coats and other winter wear this month. 100 Mile Ford is on track to raise over 100 jackets for community members in need this winter. For the past several weeks, 100 Mile Ford has been taking part in the KOT Auto Group’s eighth annual Coat Drive, the third time the dealership has participated. Carole Velne, an accountant with 100 Mile Ford, said they are looking to collect as many coats, gloves, toques and other winter accessories as possible. “For those that need a little bit more extra warmth at this time of year. We collect coats, hats, toques, mitts and scarves,” Velne said. “We pile them up into our truck and at the end of November they will all be taken out to the Cariboo Christian Life Fellowship (CCLF) church in the 108 Mile Ranch area.” As of Wednesday, Nov. 18, Velne said the Ford Ranger they’ve been storing the donations in is half full. She noted that they would welcome more donations to come in for the last few days of November. To donate, Velne said community members simply need to come by 100 Mile Ford during their regular hours of operation and drop off their donations. She noted that some have left bags of clothes by the front door when they come in to work in the morning. “We know times are tough. The economy is not booming the best right now. There’s just a lot of people out there who really can’t afford the proper warm jackets for the Cariboo weather up here,” Velne said. “Whatever little bit people can throw our way is just such a big help.” Donations will be accepted until Monday, Nov. 30. Afterwards, they’ll go to the CCLF, which will be responsible for distributing them. Velne said she is looking forward to seeing just how much winter wear they can raise. “I think whatever people have that would keep people warm would be gladly accepted.” **News** **Doerkson lays out immediate priorities, explains B.C. cabinet

e787c671119014dcfc68c88548768019.text: If your period home is heated by oil or LPG and isn’t connected to mains gas, you could currently be eligible for up to £9,000 towards an air-source or ground-source heat pump – an appealing prospect with temperatures plummeting and winter drawing near. But the additional £1,500 grant is only available until March 2027 – and if you leave the decision until your boiler breaks in the middle of winter, you may not have time to make use of it. A heat pump is not a quick replacement. Your home needs to be surveyed, the system designed around its heat loss and existing pipework, and changes such as larger radiators or a bigger hot-water cylinder may be recommended. That makes November a crucial moment to start the process. As Lewis Harding, a Gas Safe registered engineer at First Point Plumbing in New Mills, explains: "Make the call in the autumn, while the old oil boiler still runs. Once it gives out in January, most families order whatever can go in that week, because nobody wants to sit in a cold farmhouse while a heat pump is planned around the house." In other words, the grant deadline and the boiler deadline are working against each other. Wait for a midwinter breakdown and you could find yourself choosing the fastest available boiler instead, but start now, and you have time to establish whether a heat pump is suitable, compare installers and apply for the funding. Here's how to get going... An old stone farmhouse or barn conversion needs a system designed around its quirks. A survey should assess how much heat each room loses, check the existing pipework and radiators, and establish whether they can keep the rooms warm with the lower water temperatures used by most heat pumps. Some radiators may need replacing with larger models and a new hot-water cylinder could be needed. Listed buildings bring another consideration.
